Saturn V. The world's most powerful rocket ever successfully flown, standing three hundred sixty-three feet tall and capable of lifting one hundred thirty metric tons to low Earth orbit. Designed by Wernher von Braun and built by NASA in the nineteen sixties, the Saturn V launched thirteen times and remains the only launch vehicle to carry humans beyond Earth orbit, making possible the Apollo lunar missions.

The Saturn V comprised three stages. The first stage had five F-1 engines generating seven point five million pounds of thrust. The second stage used five J-2 engines, burning liquid hydrogen and oxygen in the vacuum of space. The third stage, also using J-2 engines, provided the trans-lunar injection burn. Each Saturn V was a single-use, expendable rocket standing as tall as a thirty-six-story building and was the most complex machine ever built at the time, requiring precision engineering, new materials like aluminum-lithium alloys, and computer-controlled guidance systems.

The rocket's payload included the Command and Service Module, the Lunar Module, and the Instrument Unit that guided the rocket using an inertial measurement system and onboard computer—primitive by modern standards but revolutionary in the nineteen sixties. Von Braun, a German-American rocket scientist, had dreamed of space exploration since childhood and led the entire Saturn V program from design to launch. His vision and technical mastery made the program's aggressive timeline and complex engineering manageable.

The Saturn V underwent rigorous testing. The F-1 engines had to be clustered because no single engine was powerful enough, making vibration control a critical engineering challenge validated at test stands at Marshall Space Flight Center. Only thirteen Saturn Vs were launched: eleven to support the Apollo program, with six landing on the Moon, one unmanned test launch, and one aborted Apollo thirteen mission that still safely returned its crew despite an oxygen tank explosion in transit. The cost of the Saturn V program, approximately two hundred eighty billion dollars in twenty twenty-four currency, remains the most expensive space program ever conducted, employing over four hundred thousand workers across America. After Apollo, no nation has built a rocket as powerful as the Saturn V.
